gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the $22.95 iFixit Precision Electric Screwdriver, which ChatGPT showed as the budget pick, comes with no bits: with iFixit's cheapest 4 mm bit kit it costs $42.90 for 32 bits ($1.34 per bit), and with the 64-bit Mako kit it costs $62.90, which is more than the $59.97 Fanttik E1 Max with 50 bits included. AAA cells are extra in both cases.
standout_why: I compared five pages. The cited Fanttik blog (fanttik.com HOTO vs Fanttik) gives bits per dollar for only three Fanttik models. toolengineers.com says it ran no tests and lists no prices, battery figures or per-charge figures. butactuallygood.com works out cost per bit only for kits that include bits and does not cover the iFixit driver. powertoolsinsider.com lists the iFixit Mako only as a manual driver at about $40 and never pairs it with the electric driver. Our own current page lists the iFixit driver as '4 mm bits sold separately' and gives no price for bits. None of them gives a ready-to-use total for the bit-less driver. Screws per charge does not stand out: butactuallygood and powertoolsinsider already print the E1 Max 450+ and E2 Ultra 650+ claims.
decides: This changes the budget slot, not the top pick. The iFixit driver is only cheap if you already own 4 mm bits. A buyer with no bits pays $42.90 for 32 bits plus AAA cells, which is $17.07 less than the E1 Max for 18 fewer bits, a 0.15 N·m motor, no recharging and no low/high torque choice. Paired with the Mako kit it costs $2.93 more than the E1 Max. For a first kit the RYOBI MICROTECH FVD02K ($49.97 with 50+ accessories, 0.2 N·m) or the E1 Max is the better buy. The E1 Max stays the default for delicate work because its 0.05 N·m low setting is a third of the iFixit's only electric torque (0.15 N·m).
